clue.text: Former US President — R Reagan — mistakenly ignoring a backwoodsman

indicators.note: Something done mistakenly comes out other than as intended, so these letters land in a new order.

parts.note: Two Presidents of that surname reached the White House, so the name is a straight lift.

indicators.note: To ignore a letter is to leave it out of the material entirely before anything else happens.

parts.note: This is the letter that goes: R REAGAN is told to ignore an A.
What is left of R REAGAN is R, R, E, G, A, N, and those six letters resettle.

explanation.walkthrough: Two US Presidents in one clue and neither of them is the answer: one surname is a straight lift, the other is raw material. The dashes are punctuation for the surface only.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names an outlaw who lived rough in the Australian bush, which is the kind of man a backwoodsman is.

clue.text: Wild country? Public transport heading for home

parts.note: The public transport that runs to a route number is a bus.

indicators.note: Asking for the heading of a word means taking the first letter and nothing else.

parts.note: Only the first letter of the word is taken.

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a definition that points rather than translates, and the surface is an ordinary commuter sentence about catching one home.
explanation.definitionFit: In Australia and southern Africa the word is the standard term for uncultivated backcountry, which is exactly wild country.

clue.text: Playwright's maxim about hearts

indicators.note: Here it means wrapped around: the word in front closes over the letter named next.

parts.note: A saw is an old proverb or maxim — 'many a true word', that sort of thing.
H is the card-table abbreviation for hearts.

explanation.walkthrough: A maxim about hearts sounds like a line of dialogue, which is the point: the surface is theatrical and the wordplay is a card suit inside an old word for a proverb.
explanation.definitionFit: The Irish dramatist behind Pygmalion is one of very few playwrights short enough for a four-letter light, so the definition works by example.

clue.text: List eighteen letters in reverse order

indicators.note: The letters are to be read from the far end backwards instead of the way they are written.

parts.note: A to R is a span of eighteen letters of the alphabet, so the clue writes it as A TO R.

explanation.walkthrough: Counting the alphabet is the whole trick, and 'letters' looks like part of the surface sentence rather than the instruction it is.
explanation.definitionFit: A rota is the written roster saying who is on duty when — the duty-list sense of 'list', not a catalogue or a lean.

clue.text: Note Spanish girl's standard of perfection?

definitions.note: The answer turns up only in the idiom 'dressed to the nines', so the setter defines the phrase's sense with a singular noun rather than matching the plural.

parts.note: N is the crossword shorthand for a musical note.
Inés is a common Spanish girl's name, wanted here in full.

explanation.walkthrough: An abbreviation plus a first name is one of the oldest charades going, and the question mark admits the definition is an idiom rather than a dictionary equivalent.
explanation.definitionFit: Dressed to the nines means turned out perfectly, so the plural carries the idea of the highest standard anyone could reach.

clue.text: English more authoritarian about a person from the Orient

indicators.note: It means the pieces close around what comes next, so the single letter lands between them rather than at either end.

parts.note: E is the standard abbreviation for English.
The clue's own 'a' is taken at face value as one letter.
Someone more authoritarian is sterner; the comparative form is what is wanted.

explanation.walkthrough: A sentence about strictness that is really about geography. 'More X' almost always asks for the -ER comparative spelled out, which is worth banking.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone from the Orient is an easterner in the plainest sense: a compass direction turned into a noun for a person.

clue.text: Beer initially on verge of running out? Calamity

indicators.note: It asks for the first letter of the word in front of it and nothing more.

parts.note: Only the first letter of the word is wanted.
Supplies on the verge of running out are running low.

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a pub running dry and the definition is a misfortune, so the sense wanted is 'it came as a blow', not the punch.
explanation.definitionFit: A blow is a sudden piece of bad luck that lands on you, which is the calamity sense rather than the physical strike.

clue.text: A name involved with this clue? Cape Canaveral, perhaps

indicators.note: Letters described as involved are tangled up together, so they come out in a new arrangement.

parts.note: The opening word is one of the letters.
N is the usual abbreviation for name.
The clue points at itself: its own two words supply the remaining eight letters.

explanation.walkthrough: Self-reference is the joke — the material really is the words of this clue — and the comma before 'perhaps' marks Cape Canaveral as one example rather than the thing itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Cape Canaveral is where rockets go up from, so it is a single instance of the category the answer names.

clue.text: Playwright with point about river and wasteland

indicators.note: The two named pieces close around the letter that follows, which drops in at the join.

parts.note: Oscar Wilde is the five-letter playwright setters reach for.
R is the map abbreviation for river.
A ness is a headland — the point of land running out into the sea.

explanation.walkthrough: Two playwrights turn up in this grid and this is the other one. NESS for a point is worth banking: setters use it whenever a clue goes near a coastline.
explanation.definitionFit: A wasteland is empty, uncultivated ground that nobody farms or builds on, which is what the answer names.

clue.text: Lack of coverage from tin spikes on board ship

indicators.note: Anything taken on board goes inside the vessel, so the pieces sit within the letters named next.

parts.note: SS is a steamship, and what goes aboard sits between the two letters.
A tin is a can.
The tines of a fork are its spikes.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Coverage' is clothing here rather than news or insurance, and that is what makes the definition so hard to see coming.
explanation.definitionFit: Scantiness is the state of being scanty — barely covering anything — so a lack of coverage is precisely what the noun names.

clue.text: Cow without tail? Nonsense

indicators.note: It marks the subtraction: whatever is named after it comes off the word in front.

parts.note: To cow someone is to bully them — the verb, not the animal.
A word's tail is its last letter, and that letter here is Y.

explanation.walkthrough: The farm animal is a decoy: 'cow' is a verb, so the clue is about intimidation and the question mark warns that the reading has shifted.
explanation.definitionFit: Bull is the dismissive term for nonsense — 'a load of old bull' — a polite shortening of the cruder phrase.

clue.text: Description of job, with story about cocaine — a remarkable thing

parts.note: A job spec is the description an employer writes.

indicators.note: The story is wrapped round the single letter that comes after it.

parts.note: A story is a tale.
C is the standing abbreviation for cocaine.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Spec' for a job description is modern office shorthand, and the lurid surface — a story about drugs — is exactly the sort of thing the definition covers.
explanation.definitionFit: A spectacle is something worth stopping to stare at, impressive or shocking enough to draw a crowd.

clue.text: Beats first couple of thieves with sacks

indicators.note: A couple is two, so exactly two letters are taken from the word that follows.

parts.note: Only the two letters at the front of the word are used.
To sack a city is to rob it, and the -s carries across.

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves of the surface are crime and neither is the definition: the sense wanted is the pulse, the thump of a heart or a headache.
explanation.definitionFit: A wound or a pulse that throbs beats steadily, so the verb answers 'beats' in its rhythmic, physical sense.

clue.text: Government dispute blocking blatant hospital extension beyond limits

indicators.note: To block something is to sit in the way of it, so these letters go inside the word that follows.

parts.note: Something blatant is overt — done in the open.
G stands for government, as in the American G-man.
A row is a dispute.
H is the signpost abbreviation for hospital.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Blocking' reads as bureaucratic obstruction in the surface while working as an insertion instruction, which is the neatest thing in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Overgrowth is growth that has run past the bounds set for it, an extension beyond limits like a hedge swallowing a fence.

clue.text: Puritan translation of Latin is circumspect

indicators.note: A translation delivers the same material in a different form, and here the difference is the order of the letters.

parts.note: A prude is the puritanical sort, easily shocked.
The five letters of the language come out in a new order.

explanation.walkthrough: Only half the clue is shuffled — the opening five letters are a straight synonym — and 'is' is doing nothing but joining wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Prudential means governed by prudence, weighing risks before acting, which is what a circumspect person does.

clue.text: South Africa's composer turning up in Croatian city

parts.note: ZA is South Africa's international vehicle and internet code.

indicators.note: The letters are turned, and in a down entry that means reading them from the bottom upwards.

parts.note: Alban Berg, who wrote Wozzeck, supplies four letters that are then read upwards.

explanation.walkthrough: ZA is the code on South African number plates, and Berg belongs with Bax and Arne in the drawer of very short composers setters keep handy.
explanation.definitionFit: The Croatian capital is the city meant, so the definition names it by country rather than by name.

clue.text: New take on music: bit of opera follows version, one in fashion

indicators.note: One piece following another is placed after it, so this chunk comes second rather than first.

parts.note: V is the abbreviation for version.
An aria is a self-contained number in an opera.

indicators.note: It is the insertion: the single letter drops inside the word named after it.

parts.note: The ton, from the French, is fashionable society.
I is the Roman numeral for one.

explanation.walkthrough: 'The ton' for fashionable society is Regency vocabulary that now survives mostly in crosswords, and the colon makes the whole sentence read as a music review.
explanation.definitionFit: A variation is a theme played again in altered form, which is literally a new take on a piece of music.

clue.text: Interruption popular in tours? Wrong

indicators.note: Letters that have gone wrong are letters no longer in their proper order.

parts.note: Something popular is in — the fashion sense of the word.
These seven letters, shuffled, supply everything after the opening pair.

explanation.walkthrough: The word 'in' does two jobs here, once as a synonym for popular and once as raw material, which is exactly where the letter count catches solvers out.
explanation.definitionFit: An intrusion is an unwanted arrival that breaks in on whatever was happening, which is the interruption meant.

clue.text: Green is erratic, partly reflecting amber?

indicators.note: Only a slice of the words is wanted, not the whole of any of them.
A reflection comes back the other way round, so the run of letters is read from the right.

parts.note: A run of five consecutive letters starts inside 'Green' and stops inside 'erratic'.

explanation.walkthrough: Green and amber set up a traffic light, which is the whole misdirection: the definition is the fossil sap and the letters are lying in the clue back to front.
explanation.definitionFit: Amber is fossilised tree resin, so the definition names one particular example of the answer — hence the question mark.

clue.text: Attacker offing one horseman

indicators.note: It is the setter's way of saying take off: the letter named next comes away.

parts.note: An attacker who strikes and runs is a raider.
'One' here is the indefinite article A, and that is the letter removed.

explanation.walkthrough: Attacker and horseman both suit a battlefield surface, so the definition hides in plain sight and only the letter count separates them.
explanation.definitionFit: A rider is one who rides, so horseman is the everyday synonym — the same word that names an added clause on a contract.

clue.text: Failed battery starts to endanger substantial amounts of data

indicators.note: A failed battery no longer works the way it was built, and neither do its letters.

parts.note: The seven letters of the word are the raw material for the shuffle.

indicators.note: It calls for the initial letters of the two words that follow.

parts.note: The initial letters of the two words are E and S.

explanation.walkthrough: A dead battery and a unit of storage share nothing but their letters, and 'starts to endanger' reads as a warning rather than as an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A terabyte is around a trillion bytes, so terabytes are substantial amounts of stored data by any measure.

clue.text: Races including contest chasing American cars?

indicators.note: To include something is to hold it within, so the word before opens up to take it.

parts.note: Someone who races runs, and the -s comes along with it.

indicators.note: Chasing means running along behind, so this piece is placed after the one it chases.

parts.note: A is the standard abbreviation for American.
A boxing contest is a bout.

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is motor sport and the definition is parked at the end, with the question mark conceding that not every car is one of these.
explanation.definitionFit: A runabout is a light car kept for short local journeys, so 'cars' defines the plural by the class it sits in.

clue.text: Succeeded in blocking annoying emails in abrupt movement

indicators.note: Whatever blocks a channel sits in the middle of it, which is where this letter goes.

parts.note: Unwanted marketing email is spam.
S is the genealogist's abbreviation for succeeded.

explanation.walkthrough: Spam for junk mail is recent vocabulary, and the surface — a message stopped from getting through — hides the fact that a letter is being pushed inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A spasm is a sudden involuntary jerk of a muscle, which is an abrupt movement in the most literal sense.

clue.text: Court decision offering only opening for club

parts.note: To court someone is to woo them — the verb, not the tennis or the law.

indicators.note: Handing over just its opening means the single letter at the front of the word and nothing after it.

parts.note: Only the opening letter of the word is used.

explanation.walkthrough: A courtroom ruling is the picture, and neither key word means what it seems: the courting is romantic and the club belongs on a golf course.
explanation.definitionFit: A wood is the golf club with the bulky head, once carved from persimmon, so 'club' defines it by its family.

clue.text: Prison reporting not concluded

indicators.note: It works as a subtraction sign: the word it governs is missing from the letters you are given.

parts.note: News reporting is coverage.
Something concluded is over, and those four letters are struck out of the longer word.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Over' for concluded is the pivot the whole clue turns on, and the surface reads as a newsroom bulletin rather than as an instruction to delete.
explanation.definitionFit: A cage is a barred enclosure holding a creature against its will, which is what a prison is to its inmates.

clue.text: Separate opportunity for actor

definitions.meaning: the verb for two things drawing away from each other, as a crowd does to let someone through
the role in a play that an audition is held to hand out

explanation.walkthrough: Four words and no letters move. The trick is that the two halves are different parts of speech — a verb, then a noun — so the sentence reads as one continuous phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: To part is to divide or draw apart, and a part is the role an actor is cast in: one word, a verb sense and a noun sense.

clue.text: Dam that is put back in Western Region

indicators.note: Put back means turned round, and an across answer reversed reads from the right.

parts.note: WR was British Rail's Western Region, the network running west out of Paddington.

indicators.note: It places the two letters inside the abbreviation that follows.

parts.note: 'That is' is i.e. written out, and it goes in the other way round.

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like a railway memo. British Rail's regions left crosswords a stock of two-letter abbreviations, and i.e. for 'that is' is another piece of standing kit.
explanation.definitionFit: A weir dams a river to hold the water back and control its flow, so 'Dam' names it by the job it does.

clue.text: Fix a drink, getting US lawyer a cocktail

parts.note: To fix something in place is to pin it.
The clue's own 'a' is taken as a single letter.
A cola is a drink.
The district attorney is the American prosecuting lawyer.

explanation.walkthrough: Four pieces laid end to end and the surface still reads as an order at the bar. DA comes straight from American courtroom drama and is a crossword regular.
explanation.definitionFit: The rum, pineapple and coconut mixture is one named drink, so 'a cocktail' defines it by the family it belongs to.

clue.text: Elevated area cold? Skip the top

indicators.note: To skip something is to pass over it, so the letter pointed at never joins the answer.

parts.note: A cold in the air is a chill.
The top of that word is its first letter, C.

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark warns that 'cold' is a noun here, and the instruction is dressed as friendly advice about not bothering with the summit.
explanation.definitionFit: A hill is a raised piece of ground, an elevated area that stops short of being a mountain.

clue.text: Complain train's getting rackety? Prepared to limit volume internally

indicators.note: Something rackety is rickety and shaken about, so its letters will not stay where they were put.
To limit is to bound something on both sides, so the shuffled letters close around what comes next.
It insists the extra letter lands inside the assembly rather than at either end.

parts.note: The five letters of the word go into the shuffle.
Something prepared has been made, and those four letters join the shuffle too.
V is the abbreviation for volume, as on a book spine.

explanation.walkthrough: Nine letters are shuffled and the tenth is dropped in afterwards. The answer is a formal, bookish verb: one animadverts ON something, publicly and critically.
explanation.definitionFit: To animadvert is to comment adversely, to carp at something out loud, which is a very formal way of saying complain.
